D21·x19g — 2026-09-22
rule: Never compare guard numbers across an evaluator pin move — cycles on either side are different regimes — and state the pinned handoff-bench commit in every cycle's evidence.
chose: THE PIN IS A REGIME BOUNDARY, written down while the pin is stable (sofar-c3, 2026-09-23). Three clauses. (1) Pinning eight runner modules and the hidden tests is NOT a defect to be fixed: it is what makes cycle N comparable to cycle N+1, and reproducibility across cycles is the whole point of a frozen evaluator. Today's regime is handoff-bench c628b557fd8f43ba6ec73f6ceffb04cb2588400c, pin hash 3b02d4088a6b. (2) Its cost is the ten round-1 loss rows the evaluator inherits live (note 01M35MJ0B7), and the response is NOT to move the pin: it is to build the orchestration equivalents in the evaluator's own code, which is not pinned — tasks 3.5 and 3.6. (3) WHEN THE PIN EVENTUALLY MOVES, every cycle before it belongs to a different regime: guard numbers must not be compared across that boundary, and each cycle's evidence names the pin it ran under so the boundary is visible after the fact rather than reconstructed. The same holds for the pinned agent binary, which drifts under the evaluator (the live Claude Code install reached 2.1.280 tonight while the cycle ran the frozen 2.1.273).
over: (a) Treating the inherited rows as a reason to re-pin to round 2's runner, which would buy the fixes and silently destroy comparability with every cycle already run. (b) Leaving the boundary as an understanding held by whoever was present, to be reconstructed later from commit dates. (c) Recording it only in task 3.6, where it would be read once and closed with the task.
because: The sentence is worth nothing today and a great deal the first time someone compares a pre-move cycle with a post-move one and finds a difference that is entirely harness. A pin move is invisible in the numbers it changes, so the boundary has to be written before it moves, by whoever knows the pin is stable — after the move nobody remembers to.
